prompt: Your pom declares library A and then library B. A needs Z 1.2 and B needs Z 1.5, and nothing else mentions Z. Which Z does Maven put on the classpath?

choices.text: Z 1.5, since the newer version wins a conflict
choices.why: That is Gradle's rule. Maven's is about position in the graph and never compares the versions.

choices.text: Both, each loaded by the library that asked for it
choices.why: A classpath holds one copy of a library; the tree marks the other request as omitted for conflict.
Both requests sit two steps from the project, and on a tie the one declared first wins. A comes first in the pom.

choices.text: Neither: the build stops until an exclusion picks one
choices.why: Maven resolves the conflict itself and says so only in `dependency:tree -Dverbose`; the build carries on.

prompt: How many jars did `mvn dependency:build-classpath -DincludeScope=runtime` list for the ISBN checker in lesson 1?
A `<dependency>` written with no `<scope>` element gets the scope ___.
Your code compiles against an API that the server it will be deployed to already carries. Which scope compiles against the jar and leaves it out of what runs?

choices.text: `provided`
choices.why: Present for compiling the program and its tests, absent when it runs, because the place it runs supplies it.

choices.text: `runtime`, which is for what the server supplies at run time
choices.why: The reverse: `runtime` is absent when compiling and present when running, as for a database driver the code never names.

choices.text: `test`
choices.why: The main code could not import it at all; a `test` jar is visible only to `src/test/java`.

choices.text: `compile`, with an `<exclusions>` element
choices.why: An exclusion removes a transitive library a dependency drags in, and `compile` would still ship this one.

prompt: The pom pinned seven plugins under `pluginManagement`, and `mvn dependency:tree` still ran `maven-dependency-plugin:2.8`. Why that version?

choices.text: 2.8 is the newest release on Central
choices.why: Central had 3.11.0; nothing chose 2.8 for being new.

choices.text: Goals asked for by name on the command line skip `pluginManagement` and take Maven's own versions
choices.why: Pinned there, the same goal ran as 3.11.0: `pluginManagement` applies to a goal you name too.

choices.text: The local repository held only 2.8 and Maven never re-downloads
choices.why: Maven fetches any version it is asked for and lacks; the question is which version it asked for.

choices.text: Nothing in the pom named it, so Maven 3.8.7 fell back on its own built-in list
choices.why: No phase binds the dependency plugin, so it was left out of the block; an unpinned plugin gets whatever version the running Maven carries.

prompt: Switching to another Git branch and back leaves every source file with a new date and the same bytes. What does the next `./gradlew build` do?

choices.text: Recompiles every source, since every date moved
choices.why: That is how Maven's compiler plugin decides staleness; the same `touch` would send Maven back to `javac`.

choices.text: Reports the tasks `UP-TO-DATE`
choices.why: Gradle fingerprints inputs by their contents, and the contents are what they were when the outputs were made.

choices.text: Recompiles the main code and keeps the test classes
choices.why: Nothing recompiles at all; and a real change to main would not spare the tests on dates either.

choices.text: Takes every task `FROM-CACHE`
choices.why: The build cache is for outputs that are gone, after `clean` or in a fresh clone; here they are still in `build/`.

prompt: On a machine that has never run this project, put what the first `./gradlew build` does in order.
items: Reads `distributionUrl` from `gradle-wrapper.properties`
Downloads that zip into `~/.gradle/wrapper/dists`
Compares the bytes with `distributionSha256Sum`
Compiles the build scripts and works out the task graph
Runs `compileJava`
trap: The wrapper never looks for an installed Gradle, and nothing is run from a zip before its checksum matches.

prompt: Match each word Gradle's plain console prints beside a task to what it means.

pairs.right: its inputs and outputs are as recorded, so nothing ran
its outputs were copied in from the build cache
it had no input files to read
it ran and the build stopped there

right_distractors: it ran on the daemon instead of a new JVM

prompt: You rename a public method of `IsbnCheck` that no test calls, and build. What happens to `compileTestJava`?

choices.text: It stays `UP-TO-DATE`, because no test calls that method
choices.why: Gradle does not trace which methods a test uses; it compares the public signatures as a whole.

choices.text: It runs again, because the main classes' public signatures are different
choices.why: Compile avoidance compares the ABI of what the tests compile against, not which parts the tests use; a renamed public method is a new ABI.

choices.text: It stays `UP-TO-DATE`, just as it did after the separator edit earlier in the lesson
choices.why: That edit was inside a method body, which left every signature as it was; a rename does not.

choices.text: It comes `FROM-CACHE`
choices.why: Only an input fingerprint seen before can come from the cache, and this ABI is new.

prompt: With the build cache and the configuration cache on, the second `./gradlew clean build` in lesson 2 took some tasks `FROM-CACHE`. How many?
By lesson 3's reckoning, which of these is the case where Bazel earns its cost?

choices.text: Five developers whose one Spring Boot service takes a minute to build with Maven
choices.why: That is the team the lesson says Bazel costs more than it returns for: one service, one language, a build that is already short.

choices.text: A library that has to be published to Maven Central
choices.why: Publishing to Central is what Maven and Gradle are shaped for; nothing about it calls for Bazel.

choices.text: A project whose tests ought to run on every single build
choices.why: Running every test every time is Maven's default; Bazel's selling point is the opposite, skipping tests whose inputs did not change.

choices.text: Forty teams share one repository of Java, Go and Protocol Buffers, and CI spends most of its time retesting code no commit touched
choices.why: Several of the conditions at once: many teams, languages that depend on each other, and CI time wasted on untouched code.

prompt: An action is ___ when nothing outside its declared inputs can change its result.
After `bazel test //...` printed `(cached) PASSED`, you change one line inside a method of `IsbnCheck.java` and run it again. What happens to `IsbnCheckTest`?

choices.text: It runs again
choices.why: The library the test depends on is one of the test's inputs; a new library jar is a new action key, so the cached result no longer applies.

choices.text: `(cached) PASSED`, because the test's own source file did not change
choices.why: A test result is keyed by every input, not only its source: the library, each jar and the flags count too.

choices.text: `(cached) PASSED`, because no public signature changed
choices.why: That is Gradle's compile avoidance, which decides whether to recompile; a test still runs against the new code.

choices.text: Bazel rebuilds the library and leaves the test for CI
choices.why: `bazel test` builds what is out of date and runs every test target whose key changed, here and now.

prompt: Match each file of lesson 3's Bazel project to what it holds.

pairs.right: the Bazel release Bazelisk downloads and runs
the rule sets and external jars the module depends on
what those dependencies resolved to, with each file's hash
the targets of one package

right_distractors: the outputs of the last build

prompt: `application.properties` in the jar says `server.port=7070`, `application-dev.properties` beside it says `server.port=8081`, and the jar starts with `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev` and nothing else. Which port does Tomcat take?

choices.text: 7070, because the main file is read last
choices.why: The profile file is read on top of the main one, not under it.

choices.text: 8080, because a variable chose the profile instead of an argument
choices.why: The environment is a perfectly good place to choose a profile; the profile is active either way and its file applies.
Both files are read and, where they disagree, the active profile's file wins.

choices.text: Neither: two files setting one property stop the start-up
choices.why: Boot never complains about a property set twice; it takes the stronger place and ignores the rest.

prompt: How many jars did the bookshop's first executable jar carry under `BOOT-INF/lib`?
Which of these are inside the 19 MB `bookshop-0.1.0.jar` that `repackage` produced? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The bookshop's own compiled classes
choices.why: Under `BOOT-INF/classes`, beside the libraries.

choices.text: The `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` jar
choices.why: Starters hold no code, so `repackage` leaves them out: that is why 39 lines of tree became 34 jars.

choices.text: Tomcat's `tomcat-embed-core`
choices.why: The server is a library inside the application, so it travels in `BOOT-INF/lib`.

choices.text: A Java runtime to start it with
choices.why: The jar needs a Java on the machine; nothing in it replaces one.

choices.text: `spring-boot-jarmode-tools`
choices.why: The one jar Boot adds of its own, which lesson 23 uses to split the jar into layers.

prompt: `spring-boot-starter-parent` inherits from `spring-boot-___`, whose `<dependencyManagement>` names a version for every library Boot knows how to configure.
A command-line report tool built on `spring-boot-starter` gains `spring-boot-starter-webmvc` so that it can call a REST client. Now, after printing its report, the process never exits. Why?

choices.text: `SpringApplication.run` blocks until somebody calls `System.exit`
choices.why: Without a web starter the same call returned and the JVM exited on its own; `run` does not block.

choices.text: The report is still waiting in a buffer that Boot flushes at shutdown
choices.why: The report was printed; nothing is pending, and output buffers do not keep a JVM running.

choices.text: A new starter makes Boot wait for a profile to be chosen
choices.why: No profile is ever required: with none set Boot logs that it falls back to `default` and carries on.

choices.text: Tomcat is on the classpath, so an embedded server started, and its threads waiting for connections keep the JVM alive
choices.why: The web starter's Tomcat makes its conditions hold; `main` returns and the server's threads are still there, so the JVM stays.

prompt: Match each annotation that component scanning reads to what it says about the class.

pairs.right: a bean that holds the application's rules
a bean that keeps or fetches data, whose library's exceptions Spring translates
a bean whose `@Bean` methods define further beans
a bean that answers web requests

right_distractors: a bean created anew every time it is asked for

prompt: Spring created 78 beans in one run of lesson 5's bookshop. How many of them did the bookshop's own code define, counting `bookshopApplication`?
A project adds `AuditedBookRepository` beside `InMemoryBookRepository`. Two classes out of thirty must get the audited one, and the other twenty-eight the in-memory one. Which repair matches that?

choices.text: `@Primary` on `AuditedBookRepository`
choices.why: That makes the audited store the answer for all thirty classes, not two.

choices.text: Name the two constructor parameters `auditedBookRepository`, and let the parameter name decide
choices.why: It starts, and it rests on a parameter name that a harmless-looking rename would change; and the other twenty-eight still find two candidates.

choices.text: `@Primary` on the default store, and `@Qualifier` at those two injection points
choices.why: The candidate decides the default for everybody, and each of the two consumers overrides it for itself; a qualifier wins over `@Primary`.

choices.text: Let every class take a `List<BookRepository>` and pick one
choices.why: That is for a class meant to use every candidate; here each class wants exactly one.

prompt: A request-scoped bean is injected into a singleton. What does the singleton hold in that field?

choices.text: A proxy that finds the current request's instance on each call
choices.why: The singleton outlives every request, so it cannot keep one request's object; the proxy looks the right one up whenever it is used.

choices.text: The instance of the first request, kept for ever
choices.why: That is what happens to a prototype injected into a singleton; a request-scoped bean is handed over as a proxy precisely to avoid it.

choices.text: Nothing: start-up fails because a singleton may not depend on a narrower scope
choices.why: Spring allows it and solves it with a proxy; no report is printed.

choices.text: A new instance, created every time the field is read
choices.why: Reading a field runs no code; only a method call on the proxy reaches the current request's instance.

prompt: Spring can fall back on a constructor parameter's name only because the compiler keeps it in the class file when given the flag `-___`, which Spring Boot's parent turns on.
Match each status the bookshop answered in lesson 6 to the request that got it.

pairs.right: a POST that stored a new book
`DELETE /books/1`
a POST whose body was sent without `Content-Type: application/json`
`GET /books/abc`

right_distractors: a GET for a book that is out of stock

prompt: `BookRequest` gains an optional component, `@Size(max = 500) String blurb`, with no other constraint. A client posts a valid book and leaves `blurb` out. What happens?

choices.text: A 400 with a field error on `blurb`, since a missing value has no size
choices.why: That would make every optional field mandatory; the convention is that a constraint other than `@NotNull` says nothing about `null`.

choices.text: The book is stored with a `null` blurb
choices.why: Every standard constraint treats `null` as valid and leaves it to `@NotNull`; `@Size` only judges a string that is there.

choices.text: A 400 from Jackson, as with the missing `int` price
choices.why: Jackson refuses a missing value only for a primitive; a `String` holds `null` without complaint.

choices.text: The book is stored with an empty string in `blurb`
choices.why: Jackson does not invent a value for a property that was not sent; the component is `null`.

prompt: With the two `GET` methods, the dev log said `4 mappings in 'requestMappingHandlerMapping'`. How many does it say once `BookController` also has its `@PostMapping`?
Tomcat hands every request to one `DispatcherServlet`, which routes it to your methods. The pattern is called a front ___.
The shop adds `costCents`, what it paid the supplier, to `Book`. The controller still returns `BookResponse`. What do clients of `GET /books/1` see?

choices.text: The same JSON as before
choices.why: A field reaches the API only when somebody adds it to `BookResponse`; the domain can grow without publishing anything.

choices.text: A new `costCents` property, since Jackson writes every field of the object
choices.why: Jackson writes the object it is given, and it is given a `BookResponse`, which has no such component.

choices.text: A 500, because `BookResponse.from` no longer matches `Book`
choices.why: `from` reads the components it names and compiles as before; an extra component on `Book` breaks nothing.

choices.text: The cost, but only to clients that send `Accept: application/json`
choices.why: Content negotiation picks a format, not a set of fields.

prompt: On Spring Boot 4, somebody puts `server.error.include-stacktrace=always` in `application.properties` to debug a 500. What does the next 500's body contain?

choices.text: A `trace` member with the whole stack trace
choices.why: That is what `spring.web.error.include-stacktrace=always` does; the name written here is Boot 3's.

choices.text: No trace at all: the property was renamed to `spring.web.error.*` and the old name is ignored
choices.why: Boot 4 accepts the old name without complaint and does nothing with it; `spring-boot-properties-migrator` is the module that reports such renames.

choices.text: Nothing: the application refuses to start, because it does not recognise a property in its own file
choices.why: Boot does not validate property names at start-up; an unknown one is simply never read.

choices.text: The trace, but only in the `dev` profile
choices.why: No profile is involved; the property has no effect in any of them.

prompt: Match each exception Spring MVC raised to the status the rebuilt bookshop answered with.
A class whose `@ExceptionHandler` methods apply to every controller in the application, writing what they return as the body, is annotated `@___`.
A teammate adds a handler for a persistence library's constraint-violation exception, answering 409 with `e.getMessage()` as the `detail`. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: 409 is reserved for the shop's `DuplicateIsbnException`
choices.why: A status code is not owned by one exception; a conflict with the stored state is a 409 whoever detects it.

choices.text: It makes the application fail to start with an ambiguous handler
choices.why: That happens to a second handler for an exception `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` already handles, which a library's exception is not.

choices.text: The text is the library's, written for a developer, and it hands SQL, table names and other rows' values to a stranger
choices.why: A message goes into a response only when you wrote the exception; a library's own text is for the log.

choices.text: The handled exception is logged twice
choices.why: The opposite risk: a handled exception is not logged by Spring at all, so nothing reaches the log unless the handler writes it.

prompt: A client written for the bookshop reads `type` from every error it gets. Pointed at `javalin-hello`, it asks for `GET /books/9`. What does it receive?

choices.text: The same `application/problem+json` the bookshop sends
choices.why: Problem details were lesson 7's work inside Spring; Javalin brings none of it.

choices.text: A 500, since `javalin-hello` has no JSON mapper to write the error body with
choices.why: That was the first build; with `jackson-databind` 2 in the pom, the 404 is answered without needing JSON at all.

choices.text: A 200 with an empty JSON object
choices.why: The handler throws when no book matches; it never writes an empty body.

choices.text: A 404 in plain text, `No book with id 9`, with no `type` to read
choices.why: Javalin turns `NotFoundResponse` into a plain-text 404; the problem shape exists only once somebody registers an exception handler that writes it.

prompt: On its first measured run the bookshop logged `Started BookshopApplication in 3.249 seconds`, and `first-answer.sh` reported `first answer after 4076 ms`. How many milliseconds did the client wait that Spring's own line does not count?

A team writes a function that cloud infrastructure starts on each burst of requests, so a user waits on every cold start. They want annotations and injection close to Spring's. Which fits that best, by lesson 8?

choices.text: Play, whose development mode recompiles on the next request
choices.why: Play's Java API wires with Guice at start, by reflection, the same moment Spring Boot does.

choices.text: Javalin, since it keeps Spring's conveniences without a container
choices.why: Javalin starts quickly by giving those conveniences up; injection is `new` in `main`, with no annotations at all.

choices.text: Micronaut
choices.why: Its annotation processors wire the application inside `javac`, so the start has nothing to scan or reflect on, and its annotations resemble Spring's on purpose.

choices.text: Spring Boot as the course builds it, given more memory
choices.why: Memory does not move the wiring out of the start: it is still scanning and reflection on every launch.

prompt: GraalVM's `native-image` compiles a program ahead of time into one executable, and anything the program reaches by ___ has to be declared before that build.
The `book` table holds ids 1 to 4, taken from its `bigserial` sequence. One `INSERT` is refused by the `UNIQUE` rule, the next by the `CHECK`, and a third succeeds. Which id does the third row get?
The bookshop refuses to start, and its last `Caused by` is `PSQLException: FATAL: database "shop" does not exist`. Which of these does that line establish? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL driver is on the class path
choices.why: The message is the driver's own exception; with no driver the failure would be `No suitable driver found`.

choices.text: Something accepts connections at the host and port in the URL
choices.why: A `FATAL:` line is the server answering; nothing listening would be `Connection ... refused`.

choices.text: The user name and password were accepted
choices.why: The login worked: a wrong role or password stops earlier, with `password authentication failed`.

choices.text: The `book` table exists
choices.why: Nothing got as far as a table; the database named at the end of the URL is missing altogether.

prompt: When the bookshop's code calls `close()` on a connection it borrowed from HikariCP, the connection is not closed: it goes back to the ___.
Why does the bookshop's `postgresql` dependency carry `<scope>runtime</scope>`?

choices.text: The code never names a driver class; it is needed only once the application runs
choices.why: The code compiles against `java.sql` and Spring's classes, and the driver behind those interfaces is found when the application starts.

choices.text: So that the executable jar leaves it out and the machine that runs the jar supplies its own copy
choices.why: That is `provided`. A `runtime` jar travels in `BOOT-INF/lib` exactly because the application needs it to run.

choices.text: So that tests cannot open a real database by accident
choices.why: A `runtime` dependency is on the test classpath too; scope says nothing about which database a test reaches.

choices.text: Spring Boot's parent requires it of every driver
choices.why: The parent manages the version; the scope is the project's own decision, made from what the code imports.

prompt: Inside a method marked `@Transactional(readOnly = true)`, code loads a book and calls a method that changes its price on the object. What reaches the database when the method returns?

choices.text: An `UPDATE` of the price column alone
choices.why: Even in a writing transaction Hibernate's default `UPDATE` sets every mapped column; and here dirty checking is skipped altogether.

choices.text: An `UPDATE` of every column, as with `RepriceOnce`
choices.why: `RepriceOnce.run` was a plain `@Transactional`; the read-only flag is what changes the outcome here.

choices.text: A `LazyInitializationException` at the commit
choices.why: The book is managed throughout the method; that exception is about loading a lazy field after the context closed.

choices.text: No `UPDATE`
choices.why: `readOnly` tells Hibernate nothing read here will be written back, so it skips the work of noticing changes; the new price stays in memory.

prompt: A service method returns a `Book` entity from its `@Transactional` method, and the controller then changes the book's price on the returned object. What happens to the row?

choices.text: Hibernate writes an `UPDATE` at the end of the request
choices.why: That would need a context still open and a commit after the change; the service's transaction is already over.

choices.text: Nothing: the object is detached, and no one compares it with the row any more
choices.why: When the transaction ended the persistence context closed; a change to a detached entity is never written.

choices.text: Hibernate writes the `UPDATE` at once, since every change to a loaded entity is intercepted as it happens
choices.why: Nothing runs when a field of a loaded book changes; Hibernate finds changes by comparing values at flush, and this object is no longer in any context.

choices.text: The call throws `LazyInitializationException`
choices.why: Changing a field it already holds needs no database; only loading something unloaded throws.

prompt: Match each term from lesson 10 to what it is.

pairs.right: a map, for one transaction, from each key to the one object for that row
sending the pending statements to the database
a generated subclass object that knows only the id
a query language that names entities and their fields

right_distractors: a table Hibernate creates from the entities

prompt: So that the list of books arrives with real authors instead of proxies, in one statement, the query reads `select b from Book b join ___ b.author order by b.id`.
The catalogue holds seven books. How many books are in `content` for `GET /books?size=3&page=2`?
The shop wants every book whose author is one of a given collection of names, cheapest first. Which method on `BookRepository` asks for that as a derived query?

choices.text: `List<Book> findByAuthorNameInOrderByPriceAsc(Collection<String> names)`
choices.why: `Book` has no property `price`; the startup check refuses it with `No property 'price' found`.

choices.text: `List<Book> findByAuthorNameInOrderByPriceCentsAsc(Collection<String> names)`
choices.why: The subject ends at `By`; `AuthorName` is a path through the relationship, `In` compares with any value in the collection, and `OrderBy…Asc` sorts by the field.

choices.text: `List<Book> findByAuthorNameInOrderByPrice_centsAsc(Collection<String> names)`
choices.why: A derived query names the entity's fields, never the column; `price_cents` is the table's spelling.

choices.text: `List<Book> findAuthorNameInByPriceCentsAsc(Collection<String> names)`
choices.why: Everything before the first `By` is the subject; here the condition would be read as part of it and `PriceCentsAsc` as the predicate.

prompt: A teammate writes `@Query(value = "select title from book where pric_cents < ?1", nativeQuery = true)`, with the column misspelt. When does the mistake show?

choices.text: At start-up, as with the misspelt `b.price` in JPQL
choices.why: That check parses JPQL against the entities; with `nativeQuery = true` there is no JPQL to parse.

choices.text: At compile time
choices.why: To `javac` the query is a string inside an annotation; nothing reads it until the application runs.

choices.text: At the first start, as `PropertyReferenceException`
choices.why: That exception comes from reading a derived query's method name; this method's name is not parsed at all.

choices.text: At the first call, when PostgreSQL rejects the SQL
choices.why: A native query goes to the database as SQL, and Hibernate checks nothing in it against the entities, so start-up passes.

prompt: For an endless feed, `offset` makes PostgreSQL find and discard every earlier row. ___ pagination asks instead for the rows after the last one seen, such as `where title > ?`.
Why does the controller wrap the service's `Page` in a `PagedModel` before returning it?

choices.text: `Page` is an interface for Java code; `PagedModel` is the JSON shape Spring Data keeps stable
choices.why: Returning `PagedModel` says in the method's type exactly what a client receives: `content` and the four numbers.

choices.text: Without it Spring Data would skip the `count(*)` query
choices.why: Whether the count runs is decided by the repository call; the wrapper only shapes the JSON afterwards.

choices.text: `PagedModel` caps the page size at 2000
choices.why: The cap belongs to the web support that builds the `Pageable` from the request.

choices.text: A `Page` holds entities, and `PagedModel` maps them to DTOs
choices.why: The service already mapped the entities with `Page.map`; the page that reaches the controller holds `BookResponse` records.

prompt: A book's price is the only thing changed, and the change is saved. How do the `UPDATE` statements of EBean and of Hibernate, at its default, differ?

choices.text: They are the same statement, since both end in the same JDBC calls
choices.why: Ending in JDBC says how the statement travels, not what it says; who writes the SQL decides that.

choices.text: Hibernate's names only the price column; EBean's rewrites every column of the row it loaded
choices.why: The reverse: the object that tracks its own changed properties is EBean's.

choices.text: EBean's names only the price column; Hibernate's sets every mapped column
choices.why: Enhancement lets each EBean object record which properties changed, while Hibernate by default sends one `UPDATE` per entity covering all its columns.

choices.text: EBean sends none until the persistence context flushes
choices.why: EBean has no persistence context; saving is the `DB.save(book)` call itself.

prompt: The MyBatis `search` statement from lesson 12 is called with both `title` and `maxPrice` null. What SQL reaches PostgreSQL?

choices.text: `... WHERE ORDER BY title`, which PostgreSQL refuses
choices.why: That is the bug of building the clause by hand; `<where>` exists to avoid it.

choices.text: `... WHERE title ILIKE '%' || NULL || '%'`, which matches nothing
choices.why: An `<if>` whose test fails contributes no text at all to the statement.

choices.text: Nothing: MyBatis throws because a mapper argument is null
choices.why: Null arguments are exactly what the `test` expressions are written to check.

choices.text: `SELECT title, price_cents FROM book ORDER BY title`, with no `WHERE` at all
choices.why: `<where>` writes `WHERE` only when a condition survived, and here neither `<if>` did.

prompt: `jdbi-look`'s classpath listed six jars. Leaving out the PostgreSQL driver, `slf4j-api` and `slf4j-nop`, how many jars are JDBI and what it depends on?
A `@Transactional` service method saves an order through Spring Data JPA, then inserts a report row with `JdbcClient`. The insert fails and the method throws. What happens to the order?

choices.text: It stays, since JPA and JDBC keep separate transactions
choices.why: Mixing them is safe precisely because they do not: one `DataSource`, one transaction.

choices.text: It stays, because Hibernate flushed it before the insert ran
choices.why: A flush sends statements inside the transaction; only the commit makes them permanent, and there is none.

choices.text: It is rolled back with the rest
choices.why: Both tools use the same `DataSource` and join the same transaction, so the failure undoes everything the method did.

choices.text: The application refuses to start with two persistence tools
choices.why: Nothing stops one application from using both; lesson 12 recommends it for one heavy report.

prompt: The bookshop starts against an empty database with `V1__catalogue.sql` and `V2__first_titles.sql` in its jar and `ddl-auto=validate`. Put what happens in order.
items: Flyway validates the two migrations it found
Flyway creates `flyway_schema_history`
Flyway applies version 1, then version 2
Hibernate builds its `EntityManagerFactory` and compares the entities with the tables
The log says `Tomcat started on port 8080`
trap: Flyway runs before the `EntityManagerFactory` is built, so Hibernate never sees a schema halfway through a migration.

prompt: Somebody fixed a typo in a comment inside `V2__first_titles.sql`, which production ran months ago, and production now refuses to start with a checksum mismatch. What is the right repair?

choices.text: Run Flyway's `repair`
choices.why: The edit changed nothing the database would have done, which is the case `repair` is for: it rewrites the stored checksum and runs nothing.

choices.text: Write a `V3` that repeats the comment
choices.why: A new migration is how a change to the data is corrected; here nothing in the data differs, and the mismatch on V2 would remain.

choices.text: Drop the production database and let Flyway rebuild it
choices.why: Dropping is for a database whose data does not matter, which production's always does.

choices.text: Set `baseline-on-migrate=true` and restart
choices.why: A baseline is for a database with no history table; this one has one, and the mismatch is in it.

prompt: The project adds `R__book_summary.sql`, which replaces a view. When does Flyway run it?

choices.text: Once, like a versioned migration, and then a checksum mismatch if edited
choices.why: That is the rule for `V` files; `R` files exist precisely to be edited and run again.

choices.text: Again whenever the file's contents change
choices.why: A repeatable migration has no version; it runs again each time its checksum differs from the last run.

choices.text: On every start, whether it changed or not
choices.why: Flyway compares the checksum first; an unchanged repeatable file is skipped.

choices.text: Never, because a file without a version is ignored
choices.why: Flyway reads both kinds from `db/migration`; the `R__` prefix is what marks this one.

prompt: Besides `databasechangelog`, Liquibase created `databasechangeloglock`. What is the second table for?

choices.text: Stopping two copies of an application that start at once from applying the same changeset twice
choices.why: Whoever holds the lock migrates; the other waits, and then finds nothing left to run.

choices.text: Keeping each changeset's checksum
choices.why: The `md5sum` column of `databasechangelog` holds those.

choices.text: Storing the rollback of every changeset
choices.why: Rollbacks are generated from the changeset or written beside it in the changelog.

choices.text: Locking the tables a changeset alters until the release is finished
choices.why: It locks no application table; it only guards the migration step itself.

prompt: Why does lesson 13 pass `--spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrate=true` once on a command line rather than writing it into `application.properties`?

choices.text: Flyway reads `spring.flyway.*` only from the command line
choices.why: Every `spring.flyway` property can live in `application.properties`; this one should not.

choices.text: In the file it would quietly baseline any non-empty database the application is pointed at, the wrong one included
choices.why: A baseline is a claim Flyway cannot check; made automatically, it skips migrations on a database that never had them.

choices.text: In the file it would baseline an empty database and skip V1 and V2
choices.why: On an empty database there is nothing to baseline; Flyway applies V1 and V2 as usual.

choices.text: It makes every start slower while it stays set
choices.why: Once a history table exists the setting does nothing at all; the danger is the first start against the wrong database.

prompt: PostgreSQL's `max_connections` is 100. Four copies of the bookshop run with `maximum-pool-size=10` each. How many connections are left for every other client of that server?

An order's first line has already lowered a stock when its second line throws `OutOfStockException`. Which of these changes to `OrderService` would leave work from that order in the database? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `place` catches `OutOfStockException` and returns normally
choices.why: Returning normally tells the proxy all went well, and it commits what ran before the throw.

choices.text: `OutOfStockException` is made a checked exception that `place` declares
choices.why: By default Spring commits when a checked exception leaves the method.

choices.text: `take` throws `IllegalStateException` instead
choices.why: That is still a `RuntimeException`, so the proxy rolls back as before.

choices.text: `place` loses `@Transactional`, and each line calls `books.save(book)` straight after `take`
choices.why: With no transaction around `place`, each `save` runs in a short transaction of its own and commits the first line's stock before the second line throws.

prompt: Inside `place`, a call to another bean runs with `REQUIRES_NEW` to record the attempt. While that call runs, how many pool connections does the request hold?

choices.text: One, shared by both transactions
choices.why: One connection carries one transaction at a time; a second transaction needs a second connection.

choices.text: One, because the suspended transaction hands its connection back to the pool
choices.why: Suspended is not finished; it is resumed on the same connection when the inner call returns.

choices.text: Two
choices.why: The caller's transaction is suspended, not ended, and keeps its connection while the new one borrows a second.

choices.text: None until the inner call commits
choices.why: A transaction borrows its connection when it begins, not when it commits.

prompt: Instead of the lock, the shop tries `update book set stock = stock - 1 where id = 3 and stock >= 1`, and the database answers that 0 rows were updated. What does that mean?

choices.text: Another transaction holds the row at that moment, so the update was skipped over
choices.why: A plain update waits for a row another transaction holds; it does not skip it.

choices.text: The `CHECK (stock >= 0)` constraint refused the row
choices.why: A refused constraint is an error, not a count of zero; here the `where` simply matched nothing.

choices.text: It is a lost update, and the stock is now wrong
choices.why: The arithmetic happens in the database on the locked row, which is exactly what rules a lost update out.

choices.text: There were not enough copies, and the stock was left as it was
choices.why: The condition is checked on the row the update locks anyway; zero rows is the refusal, which the code turns into an out-of-stock answer.

prompt: Which anomaly can never happen in PostgreSQL, even in a transaction that asks for `READ UNCOMMITTED`?

choices.text: A non-repeatable read
choices.why: That is allowed at `READ COMMITTED`, where each statement sees what was committed when it began.

choices.text: A phantom
choices.why: Only `SERIALIZABLE` rules phantoms out in the standard's table, and nothing raised the level here.

choices.text: A dirty read
choices.why: PostgreSQL accepts `READ UNCOMMITTED` and treats it as `READ COMMITTED`, so another transaction's uncommitted change is never seen.

choices.text: A lost update
choices.why: Lesson 14 produced one on purpose at `READ COMMITTED`, by taking the lock out.

prompt: A client sends an expired token with `GET /books/1`, a request that `permitAll()` lets anybody make. What does it get?

choices.text: 200, since the book is public
choices.why: The rule would allow an anonymous request; this one is not anonymous, it carries a token that fails its check.

choices.text: 403, since the token no longer grants a scope
choices.why: 403 is for a valid token without the authority; an expired token never gets as far as the rules.

choices.text: 200 for another 60 seconds, then 401

prompt: Which claims does the bookshop's `TokenController` put in a token? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `jti`, an id for revoking it

choices.text: `scope`, the user's authorities

choices.text: the password's bcrypt hash

choices.text: Yes: arguments are evaluated before `debug` is called, and only the formatting is skipped

choices.text: PostgreSQL takes the new password on its next start
choices.why: The variable is ignored once the data directory exists; changing the password means changing the role inside the database.

choices.text: Compose refuses to start, as with a missing variable
choices.why: `:?` refuses an empty value, not a changed one; both containers start.

choices.text: The application is refused at login: the database kept the old one
choices.why: The PostgreSQL image reads `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` only when it creates the database on an empty volume; the role keeps the password it was made with.

choices.text: Flyway notices the changed variable and recreates the database with the new password
choices.why: Flyway migrates the schema inside a database it can log in to; it creates neither roles nor passwords.

prompt: `docker compose stop app` stops the bookshop built with the exec-form `ENTRYPOINT`. Put what happens in order.
items: Docker sends SIGTERM to PID 1, which is Java
Each Tomcat stops accepting connections and waits for the requests already running
The JPA `EntityManagerFactory` is closed
The connection pool shuts down, closing its connections to PostgreSQL
The container exits with code 143
trap: The entity manager closes before the pool, so PostgreSQL sees its connections closed rather than dropped.

prompt: To give Hibernate more room, somebody changes the Dockerfile to `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=100` in the 1 GiB container. What is the risk?

choices.text: Memory outside the heap pushes the process over the limit, and the kernel kills it with no shutdown at all
choices.why: Class metadata, thread stacks, JIT code and network buffers live outside the heap; with the heap sized to the whole limit, nothing is left for them.

choices.text: None: the JVM never uses more than its heap
choices.why: The heap is not all the JVM uses, which is exactly why the course leaves a quarter of the limit outside it.

choices.text: The JVM ignores the limit and sizes the heap from the whole machine
choices.why: The JVM reads the container's limit and believes it; only the share of it changes.

choices.text: Docker refuses to start a container whose heap equals its limit
choices.why: Docker knows nothing about heaps; the trouble arrives at run time, when the process grows.
